expected.question_text: A newborn infant is born to a 19-year-old female. The infant's birth weight is 3.4 kg (7 lb 8 oz). Vital signs reveal marked hypotension. Neonatal examination reveals ambiguous genitalia consisting of a fused labia and an enlarged clitoris. Laboratory studies reveal: | Test | Patient's Value | Reference Range | |---|---|---| | Sodium | 132 mEq/L | 136–145 mEq/L | | Potassium | 5.2 mEq/L | 3.5–5.1 mEq/L | | Chloride | 103 mEq/L | 98–107 mEq/L | | Bicarbonate | 27 mEq/L | 22–29 mEq/L | The most likely etiology of this newborn's hypotension is
expected.explanation_footer:
This patient likely has congenital adrenal hyperplasia , as suggested by her hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and ambiguous genitalia at birth. The most common cause of CAH is a deficiency of the 21-hydroxylase enzyme , which accounts for > 95% of cases. Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase results in reduced or absent conversion of progesterone to deoxycorticosterone, ultimately leading to decreased or absent aldosterone production. It also causes decreased or absent conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol, which ultimately leads to decreased or absent cortisol production. The absence of 21-hydroxylase causes a loss of negative feedback from decreased cortisol synthesis, thereby increasing adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation and androgen production. Infants born with CAH are categorized into classic or non-classic forms. In the classic form, the androgen excess in utero causes females to be born with atypical genitalia, including clitoral enlargement and labial fusion. Males with classic CAH typically have normal-appearing genitalia at birth. Patients with the classic form often experience precocious puberty and have a higher risk of developing adrenal crisis. The non-classic form may be asymptomatic or may present as precocious puberty, hirsutism, or menstrual irregularity in women. CAH is managed with hydrocortisone, mineralocorticoids, and sodium chloride supplements. If a patient presents in adrenal crisis, they receive glucocorticoids at stress doses. Frequent monitoring is required to adjust the doses. Management can also include surgery for females with atypical genitalia. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is characterized by hypotension, hyperkalemia, and increased renin activity, as well as masculinization and female pseudohermaphroditism.
